---
title: "Quiz: matching descriptors"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Nearest-neighbour matching gives every point of image 1 a partner. Why is that a problem?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Is every point of image 1 visible and detected in image 2?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Many points have no true partner: they lie outside the overlap, or the detector did not fire there in image 2. Nearest-neighbour matching still pairs them with something, so most of its matches can be wrong (24 % correct in the demo scene).
:::

---

**Q2.** Match A has $d_1 = 0.20$, $d_2 = 0.60$; match B has $d_1 = 0.30$, $d_2 = 0.32$. Which passes the ratio test at 0.8, and what is B probably?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compute the ratios.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A: 0.33, accepted. B: 0.94, rejected: two descriptors of image 2 are almost equally close, as on a repetitive texture or a common-looking corner. Its nearest is a coin toss.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why is the ratio $d_1/d_2$ a better criterion than $d_1$ alone?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Are all features equally distinctive?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Distinctive features have large distances to all impostors, ordinary ones small distances. A single threshold on $d_1$ cannot serve both. $d_2$ measures how close the impostors of **this** feature come, so the ratio is a per-feature threshold.
:::

---

**Q4.** What does the mutual check remove that the ratio test can miss?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look at it from image 2.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Several points of image 1 picking the same point of image 2 (each with a fine ratio). The mutual check keeps only the pair where the point of image 2 picks the point of image 1 back.
:::

---

**Q5.** 250 matches are accepted, 210 of them correct, and 400 correct matches were possible. Precision and recall?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Correct over accepted, correct over possible.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Precision $210/250 = 0.84$, recall $210/400 = 0.525$.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why do exact k-d trees not help for 128-dimensional descriptors?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many neighbouring cells does the search ball reach?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In high dimensions the nearest neighbour is hardly nearer than the others, so the ball around the query reaches very many cells and backtracking visits almost all leaves: no faster than brute force. Approximate search with a fixed leaf budget trades a few wrong neighbours for speed.
:::

---

**Q7.** A culture is imaged at two time points with a stage drift. Which matches are correct as descriptors but wrong for the drift?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What moves besides the stage?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Matches on cells that moved or divided between the time points: the descriptor finds the same cell, but its displacement is not the drift. Geometry (RANSAC in the next unit) treats them as outliers if the static background provides enough matches.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that mutual nearest-neighbour pairs never share a point.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Assume $(i, j)$ and $(i, j')$ are both mutual.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If $(i, j)$ is mutual, $j$ is $i$'s nearest; if $(i, j')$ is mutual, $j'$ is $i$'s nearest. With a unique nearest neighbour, $j = j'$. The same argument from the other side shows that no $j$ is in two pairs. So the mutual pairs form a matching.
:::
